How many atoms of oxygen are present in 3.2 g of SO2? (S = 32, O = 16, NA = 6.022 × 10^23)
9::Science::atoms-molecules-exemplar.solution: Molar mass of SO2 = 32 + 2(16) = 64 g/mol. Moles of SO2 = 3.2/64 = 0.05 mol. One molecule of SO2 has 2 oxygen atoms. Number of O atoms = 0.05 × 2 × 6.022 × 10^23 = 6.022 × 10^22.

9::Science::atoms-molecules-exemplar.q: What is the law of constant proportions? Give an example.
9::Science::atoms-molecules-exemplar.solution: The law states that a chemical compound always contains the same elements in the same proportion by mass. Example: water always contains hydrogen and oxygen in mass ratio 1:8 (2g H to 16g O). No matter the source of water, this ratio remains constant.

9::Science::atoms-molecules-exemplar.q: How many molecules are present in 88 g of CO2? (C = 12, O = 16, NA = 6.022 × 10^23)
9::Science::atoms-molecules-exemplar.solution: Molar mass of CO2 = 12 + 2(16) = 44 g/mol. Moles = 88/44 = 2 mol. Number of molecules = 2 × 6.022 × 10^23 = 1.204 × 10^24.

9::Science::atoms-molecules-exemplar.q: Define relative atomic mass and molecular mass.
9::Science::atoms-molecules-exemplar.solution: Relative atomic mass: mass of an atom compared to 1/12 of mass of carbon-12 atom. Example: Na = 23 (sodium atom is 23 times heavier than 1/12 of C-12). Relative molecular mass: sum of relative atomic masses of all atoms in a molecule. Example: H2O = 1 + 1 + 16 = 18.

9::Science::motion-exemplar.q: A car accelerates uniformly from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 5 seconds. Calculate acceleration and distance covered.
Define velocity and speed. A boy walks 4 km in 2 hours. Calculate both.
9::Science::motion-exemplar.solution: Speed is distance/time = 4/2 = 2 km/h. Velocity is displacement/time. If displacement is also 4 km in same direction, velocity = 2 km/h in that direction. If he returns to origin, displacement = 0, velocity = 0.

9::Science::motion-exemplar.q: An object is thrown upward with initial velocity 20 m/s. Find maximum height and time to return (g = 10 m/s²).
9::Science::motion-exemplar.solution: At max height, v = 0. Using v² = u² - 2gh: 0 = 400 - 2(10)h. So h = 20 m. Time to max height: v = u - gt: 0 = 20 - 10t, so t = 2 s. Total time to return = 2 × 2 = 4 s.

9::Science::motion-exemplar.q: A ball is dropped from height 45 m. How long does it take to reach ground? (g = 10 m/s²)
9::Science::motion-exemplar.solution: Using s = (1/2)gt²: 45 = (1/2)(10)t². So 45 = 5t², giving t² = 9, thus t = 3 s.

9::Science::motion-exemplar.q: State Newton's first law and explain with example.
9::Science::motion-exemplar.solution: Newton's first law: an object at rest stays at rest and object in motion continues with constant velocity unless acted upon by external force. Example: passengers jerk forward when bus suddenly stops because body tends to continue forward motion due to inertia.

9::Science::gravitation-exemplar.q: Calculate the gravitational force between two masses 5 kg and 10 kg separated by 2 m. (G = 6.67 × 10^-11 N·m²/kg²)
Why is the weight of an object less on the moon than on Earth?
9::Science::gravitation-exemplar.solution: Weight is W = mg, where g depends on mass and radius of celestial body: g = GM/R². Moon has smaller mass and radius than Earth, so g_moon = 1.6 m/s² while g_earth = 10 m/s². Thus weight on moon is 1/6 of weight on Earth.

9::Science::gravitation-exemplar.q: A body weighs 50 N on Earth. What is its mass? (g = 10 m/s²)
9::Science::gravitation-exemplar.solution: Weight W = mg. So m = W/g = 50/10 = 5 kg. The mass remains 5 kg anywhere (on Earth, moon, space).

9::Science::gravitation-exemplar.q: State the universal law of gravitation.
9::Science::gravitation-exemplar.solution: Every object attracts every other object with force proportional to product of their masses and inversely proportional to square of distance between them. Mathematically: F = G(m1 × m2)/r², where G is gravitational constant.

9::Science::gravitation-exemplar.q: If Earth's mass is 6 × 10^24 kg and radius is 6.4 × 10^6 m, calculate g at Earth's surface.

10::Mathematics::real-numbers-exemplar.q: Use Euclid's division algorithm to find HCF of 135 and 225.

10::Mathematics::real-numbers-exemplar.solution: Assume 3√2 is rational. Then 3√2 = p/q where GCD(p,q) = 1. So √2 = p/(3q). Since p/(3q) is rational (ratio of integers), √2 would be rational. But √2 is irrational, contradiction. Therefore 3√2 is irrational.
Let x = 0.6̄. Then 10x = 6.6̄. Subtracting: 10x - x = 6, so 9x = 6, giving x = 6/9 = 2/3.
Using HCF × LCM = product of numbers: 4 × LCM = 96 × 404. LCM = (96 × 404)/4 = 96 × 101 = 9696.

10::Mathematics::real-numbers-exemplar.q: If HCF(a, b) = 8 and a × b = 2048, find LCM(a, b).
10::Mathematics::real-numbers-exemplar.solution: Using HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b: 8 × LCM = 2048. LCM = 256.

10::Mathematics::polynomials-exemplar.q: Find quotient and remainder when x^4 - 3x^2 + 4x + 5 is divided by x^2 - 1.
10::Mathematics::polynomials-exemplar.solution: Using polynomial long division: x^4 - 3x^2 + 4x + 5 = (x^2 - 1)(x^2 - 2) + (4x + 7). Quotient = x^2 - 2, Remainder = 4x + 7.

10::Mathematics::polynomials-exemplar.q: If α and β are zeros of x^2 - 5x + 6, find α + β and αβ.
10::Mathematics::polynomials-exemplar.solution: For ax^2 + bx + c: sum of zeros = -b/a, product = c/a. Here a = 1, b = -5, c = 6. So α + β = 5, αβ = 6. (Factoring: (x - 2)(x - 3), zeros are 2 and 3.)

10::Mathematics::polynomials-exemplar.q: Find a quadratic polynomial whose zeros are 3 and -7.
10::Mathematics::polynomials-exemplar.solution: Sum = 3 + (-7) = -4, Product = 3 × (-7) = -21. Polynomial: x^2 - (sum)x + product = x^2 - (-4)x + (-21) = x^2 + 4x - 21.

10::Mathematics::polynomials-exemplar.q: If p(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 11x - 6 and one zero is 1, find all zeros.
10::Mathematics::polynomials-exemplar.solution: Since p(1) = 1 - 6 + 11 - 6 = 0, (x - 1) is a factor. Dividing: p(x) = (x - 1)(x^2 - 5x + 6) = (x - 1)(x - 2)(x - 3). Zeros are 1, 2, 3.

10::Mathematics::pair-linear-equations-e.q: Solve graphically: x + y = 4 and 2x - y = 2.
10::Mathematics::pair-linear-equations-e.solution: From x + y = 4: y = 4 - x. Points: (0,4), (4,0). From 2x - y = 2: y = 2x - 2. Points: (0,-2), (1,0). Lines intersect at (2,2). Solution: x = 2, y = 2.
Add equations: 8x = 12, so x = 3/2. Substitute: 3(3/2) + 2y = 8. So 9/2 + 2y = 8, giving 2y = 7/2, thus y = 7/4.

10::Mathematics::pair-linear-equations-e.q: Solve using substitution: x + 2y = 7 and 2x - y = 4.
10::Mathematics::pair-linear-equations-e.solution: From first: x = 7 - 2y. Substitute in second: 2(7 - 2y) - y = 4. So 14 - 4y - y = 4, giving 5y = 10, thus y = 2. Then x = 7 - 4 = 3.

10::Mathematics::pair-linear-equations-e.q: For what value of k does the system 2x + 3y = 5 and kx + 6y = 10 have infinite solutions?
10::Mathematics::pair-linear-equations-e.solution: For infinite solutions: a1/a2 = b1/b2 = c1/c2. So 2/k = 3/6 = 5/10. From 3/6 = 1/2, we need 2/k = 1/2, thus k = 4.

10::Mathematics::pair-linear-equations-e.q: Two angles are supplementary. If one is 20° more than the other, find both angles.
10::Mathematics::pair-linear-equations-e.solution: Let angles be x and x + 20. Since supplementary: x + (x + 20) = 180. So 2x + 20 = 180, giving x = 80. Angles are 80° and 100°.

10::Mathematics::quadratic-equations-exe.q: Find nature of roots of x^2 - 6x + 9 = 0 without solving.
10::Mathematics::quadratic-equations-exe.solution: Discriminant Δ = b^2 - 4ac = 36 - 36 = 0. Since Δ = 0, roots are real and equal.

10::Mathematics::quadratic-equations-exe.q: If α and β are roots of x^2 + 3x - 4 = 0, find α^2 + β^2.
A number exceeds its positive square root by 12. Find the number.
10::Mathematics::quadratic-equations-exe.solution: Let number be x. Then x - √x = 12. Let √x = y, so y^2 - y - 12 = 0. Factoring: (y - 4)(y + 3) = 0. So y = 4 (taking positive). Thus x = 16.

10::Mathematics::arithmetic-progressions.q: If first term a = 5 and common difference d = 3, find 10th term.
Find sum of first 20 terms of AP: 2, 5, 8, 11, ...

10::Mathematics::arithmetic-progressions.solution: If 3 means are inserted, sequence is 5, A1, A2, A3, 21 (5 terms total). Common difference d = (21 - 5)/(5 - 1) = 16/4 = 4. So means are 9, 13, 17.

10::Mathematics::arithmetic-progressions.q: Find sum of all two-digit natural numbers divisible by 4.
If sum of n terms of AP is 3n^2 + 5n, find the AP.

10::Mathematics::triangles-exemplar.q: In triangle ABC, DE || BC. If AD = 3 cm, DB = 2 cm, AE = 4.5 cm, find EC.
10::Mathematics::triangles-exemplar.solution: By basic proportionality theorem (Thales): AD/DB = AE/EC. So 3/2 = 4.5/EC. Thus EC = (4.5 × 2)/3 = 9/3 = 3 cm.

10::Mathematics::triangles-exemplar.q: Two isosceles triangles have equal angles. Are they similar? Justify.
10::Mathematics::triangles-exemplar.solution: Yes. In isosceles triangle, if vertex angle is equal, base angles are also equal (property of isosceles triangle). If all angles are equal, triangles are similar by AA criterion.

10::Mathematics::triangles-exemplar.q: Triangles ABC and PQR are similar with AB/PQ = 2/3. If area of ABC is 36 cm², find area of PQR.
10::Mathematics::triangles-exemplar.solution: Ratio of areas = (ratio of corresponding sides)². Area of PQR/Area of ABC = (PQ/AB)^2 = (3/2)^2 = 9/4. So Area of PQR = 36 × 9/4 = 81 cm².

10::Mathematics::triangles-exemplar.q: In a right triangle, altitude from right angle to hypotenuse divides it into segments 2 cm and 8 cm. Find the altitude.
10::Mathematics::triangles-exemplar.solution: Altitude h from right angle to hypotenuse: h² = product of segments = 2 × 8 = 16. So h = 4 cm.

10::Mathematics::triangles-exemplar.q: Prove that if two triangles have equal areas and one pair of sides equal, then altitudes to those sides are equal.
10::Mathematics::triangles-exemplar.solution: Area = (1/2) × base × height. If areas are equal and bases (sides) are equal, then heights must be equal. A1 = (1/2)b1h1, A2 = (1/2)b2h2. If A1 = A2 and b1 = b2, then h1 = h2.

10::Mathematics::coordinate-geometry-exe.q: Find the midpoint of line segment joining (5, -3) and (3, 7).
Find slope of line joining (2, 5) and (4, 9).
Find equation of line with slope 3 passing through (1, 2).
10::Mathematics::coordinate-geometry-exe.solution: Using point-slope form: y - y1 = m(x - x1). So y - 2 = 3(x - 1). Simplifying: y = 3x - 1.

10::Mathematics::coordinate-geometry-exe.q: If vertices of triangle are (0, 0), (4, 0), (0, 3), find area.

10::Science::chemical-reactions-exemplar.q: What is a chemical reaction? Classify the reaction: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O.
10::Science::chemical-reactions-exemplar.solution: Chemical reaction is transformation of substances resulting in formation of new substances with different properties. The reaction 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O is a combination reaction (two or more reactants combine to form one product). It is also an exothermic reaction (heat is released).

10::Science::chemical-reactions-exemplar.q: Distinguish between displacement and double displacement reactions.
10::Science::chemical-reactions-exemplar.solution: Displacement reaction: A + BC → AC + B (one element displaces another). Example: Fe + CuSO4 → FeSO4 + Cu. Double displacement: AB + CD → AD + CB (two compounds exchange ions). Example: AgNO3 + NaCl → AgCl (ppt) + NaNO3.

10::Science::chemical-reactions-exemplar.q: Balance the chemical equation: Fe + Cl2 → FeCl3.
10::Science::chemical-reactions-exemplar.solution: Iron has 3 electrons in valence, chlorine takes 1. So Fe forms FeCl3. Left: 1 Fe, 2 Cl. Right: 1 Fe, 3 Cl. Balance: 2Fe + 3Cl2 → 2FeCl3.

10::Science::chemical-reactions-exemplar.q: What is decomposition reaction? Give one example.
10::Science::chemical-reactions-exemplar.solution: Decomposition reaction is breaking down of one compound into two or more simpler substances. Example: 2H2O → 2H2 + O2 (when electricity is passed, electrolytic decomposition). Another: CaCO3 → CaO + CO2 (thermal decomposition).

10::Science::chemical-reactions-exemplar.q: Write balanced equation for combustion of methane and classify it.
10::Science::chemical-reactions-exemplar.solution: CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O. Combustion is a reaction where a substance burns in oxygen, releasing heat and light. This is exothermic (heat releasing) and oxidation-reduction (redox) reaction.

10::Science::acids-bases-salts-exemplar.q: Distinguish between acid and base with one property each.
10::Science::acids-bases-salts-exemplar.solution: Acid: sour taste, turns blue litmus red, pH < 7, example HCl. Base: bitter taste, turns red litmus blue, pH > 7, example NaOH. Acid + Base → Salt + Water (neutralization).

10::Science::acids-bases-salts-exemplar.q: Calculate pH of solution with H+ ion concentration 10^-5 mol/L.
What is salt? Name three salts and write their chemical formulas.
10::Science::acids-bases-salts-exemplar.solution: Salt is ionic compound formed by neutralization of acid and base. Examples: (1) Sodium chloride NaCl, (2) Potassium nitrate KNO3, (3) Calcium sulfate CaSO4.

10::Science::acids-bases-salts-exemplar.q: Write balanced equation for reaction between HCl and NaOH. Identify type of reaction.
10::Science::acids-bases-salts-exemplar.solution: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O. This is neutralization reaction (acid-base reaction). H+ + OH- → H2O. It is also exothermic (heat is released).

10::Science::acids-bases-salts-exemplar.q: What is meant by pH? Why is pH important for living organisms?
10::Science::acids-bases-salts-exemplar.solution: pH is measure of acidity or alkalinity of solution. pH = -log[H+]. Scale 0-14: <7 acidic, 7 neutral, >7 basic. Important because: enzymes work at specific pH, blood pH must be 7.35-7.45 for life, soil pH affects plant growth, stomach needs pH 1.5-3.5 for digestion.

10::Science::light-exemplar.q: A light ray hits a plane mirror at 30° to the normal. What is angle of reflection?
10::Science::light-exemplar.solution: By law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection. If light hits at 30° to normal (i = 30°), then angle of reflection r = 30°.

10::Science::light-exemplar.q: An object is placed 15 cm from a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. Find image position and nature.
10::Science::light-exemplar.solution: Using mirror formula: 1/f = 1/u + 1/v. 1/10 = 1/15 + 1/v. So 1/v = 1/10 - 1/15 = (3-2)/30 = 1/30. Thus v = 30 cm. Since v is positive and real, image is real, inverted, enlarged, located at 30 cm in front of mirror.

10::Science::light-exemplar.q: Define refractive index. If light travels 2 × 10^8 m/s in a medium, find refractive index.
10::Science::light-exemplar.solution: Refractive index n = speed of light in vacuum / speed of light in medium = c/v. n = (3 × 10^8)/(2 × 10^8) = 1.5. The medium is glass-like.

10::Science::light-exemplar.q: A light ray enters glass slab (n = 1.5) from air at 60° to normal. Find angle of refraction.
10::Science::light-exemplar.solution: Using Snell's law: n1 sin θ1 = n2 sin θ2. 1 × sin 60° = 1.5 × sin θ2. So sin θ2 = (√3/2)/1.5 = √3/3 ≈ 0.577. Thus θ2 ≈ 35.3°.

10::Science::light-exemplar.q: Explain why objects in water appear closer than they actually are.
10::Science::light-exemplar.solution: Water has refractive index 1.33 > 1 (air). When light travels from water to air (less dense to more dense), it bends away from normal. Our eyes receive refracted rays and perceive image at apparent position closer than actual position. This is due to refraction.

10::Science::electricity-exemplar.q: Calculate current when 100 C of charge flows in 4 seconds.
A bulb rated 60 W, 230 V is operated at rated voltage. Calculate resistance and current.
Three resistors 2 Ω, 3 Ω, 6 Ω are connected in parallel. Find equivalent resistance.
A wire has resistance 10 Ω at 0°C. If temperature coefficient α = 0.005 /°C, find resistance at 50°C.
Two cells of EMF 1.5 V each are connected in series. Find total EMF and total internal resistance if each has internal resistance 0.5 Ω.
10::Science::electricity-exemplar.solution: Total EMF = 1.5 + 1.5 = 3 V. Total internal resistance = 0.5 + 0.5 = 1 Ω.

11::Mathematics::sets-exemplar.q: If A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {3, 4, 5, 6}, find A ∩ B and A ∪ B.
11::Mathematics::sets-exemplar.solution: A ∩ B = {3, 4} (common elements). A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} (all elements).

11::Mathematics::sets-exemplar.q: If U = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} is universal set and A = {1, 3, 5}, find A'.
Verify De Morgan's law: (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B' using A = {1, 2}, B = {2, 3}, U = {1, 2, 3, 4}.
If n(A) = 30, n(B) = 40, n(A ∩ B) = 10, find n(A ∪ B).
In a survey, 50 students like tea, 60 like coffee, 20 like both. How many like at least one?

11::Physics::units-measurements-exemplar.q: Express 5000 g in kg and mg.
Check dimensionally if equation v = u + at is correct.
11::Physics::units-measurements-exemplar.solution: LHS: v has dimension [LT^-1]. RHS: u is [LT^-1], at = [LT^-2][T] = [LT^-1]. LHS = RHS dimensionally. Equation is dimensionally correct.

11::Physics::units-measurements-exemplar.q: What is significant figures? Round 23.456 to 3 significant figures.
11::Physics::units-measurements-exemplar.solution: Significant figures are all digits that carry meaningful information about precision. 23.456 rounded to 3 SF = 23.5 (keeping 2, 3, 5 and rounding up last digit 4 to 5).

12::Physics::current-electricity-exempla.q: A wire of resistance R is bent into a circle. What is equivalent resistance between two diametrically opposite points?
12::Physics::current-electricity-exempla.solution: The circle is divided into two semicircles by the diameter. Each semicircle has resistance R/2. They are in parallel: Req = (R/2 × R/2)/(R/2 + R/2) = (R^2/4)/(R) = R/4.

12::Physics::current-electricity-exempla.q: A battery of EMF 6 V and internal resistance 1 Ω is connected to external resistance 5 Ω. Find terminal voltage.
12::Physics::current-electricity-exempla.solution: I = EMF/(r + R) = 6/(1 + 5) = 1 A. Terminal voltage V = EMF - Ir = 6 - 1(1) = 5 V.

12::Physics::current-electricity-exempla.q: Two cells of EMF 1.5 V and 2 V with internal resistances 0.5 Ω and 1 Ω are connected in parallel. Find equivalent EMF.
A potentiometer wire of length 100 cm has resistance 10 Ω. If a cell of EMF 1.5 V produces balance at 60 cm, find internal resistance of cell when external resistance is 5 Ω.
12::Physics::current-electricity-exempla.solution: Resistance of 100 cm = 10 Ω, so resistance of 60 cm = 6 Ω. At balance: E = I × Rext where I passes through 6 Ω section. E × 5/(r + 5) = 1.5 × (60/100). Solving for r gives internal resistance.

12::Physics::current-electricity-exempla.q: How many electrons pass through a conductor if current of 2 A flows for 10 seconds?
12::Physics::current-electricity-exempla.solution: Q = I × t = 2 × 10 = 20 C. Number of electrons = Q/e = 20/(1.6 × 10^-19) = 1.25 × 10^20 electrons.
